name_en: Shan Lin Xi High Mountain Oolong
processing: Lightly oxidised (roughly 15–20%), ball-rolled and dried without roasting; a few growers also make a gently roasted version that keeps the cool mountain character.
harvest_season: Spring (late April to May) and winter (October to November); winter lots are often praised for a thicker, cleaner cup and spring lots for aroma.
appearance_dry: Tight, glossy deep-green balls with a bluish cast and short pale stems.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow with a green edge, bright and clear.
appearance_wet: Thick whole leaves open to a vivid green with a thin red margin and a fresh, piney smell.
taste_profile: Fresh white flowers and a pine-and-cucumber coolness up front, then a thick, sweet body from the third steep and a long cooling aftertaste that Taiwanese drinkers call mountain qi.

brewing.notes: Water just off the boil and a slightly longer first steep to open the balls, then keep the next few short. Good lots have a crisp edge without bitterness; if it turns bitter, the steeps are too long.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest and sub-area: the spring and winter crops of the current year, in vacuum-sealed 150 g packs, with Long Feng Xia lots priced at the top and Yang Keng, Liu Shui Keng and Fan Zai Tian below. It is a fresh tea, best within a year of picking; lightly roasted versions keep a little longer.
description:
Shan Lin Xi, 'cedar forest stream', is a high-mountain tea area in Zhushan Township, Nantou, with gardens from about 1,200 to 1,900 metres along the road to the Sun Link Sea forest recreation area. The slopes are wrapped in conifer forest and afternoon fog, and the tea tastes like the place: cool, clean and faintly resinous where Alishan is soft and milky.

The leaf is Qing Xin oolong, lightly oxidised, ball-rolled and dried without roasting, the standard high-mountain recipe. Sub-areas carry their own reputations and prices: Long Feng Xia at the top, around 1,700 to 1,900 metres, is the most sought after, with Yang Keng, Liu Shui Keng and Fan Zai Tian below it. A few growers also make a gently roasted version that keeps the mountain character but adds a nutty warmth.

In the cup it opens with fresh white flowers and a pine-and-cucumber coolness, then a thick, sweet body arrives around the third steep, followed by the long cooling aftertaste that Taiwanese drinkers call mountain qi. It is less sweet-creamy than Li Shan and more lively; good lots have a crisp edge without bitterness. Brew with water just off the boil and a slightly longer first steep to open the balls, then keep the next few short.

It is sold by harvest, spring and winter, with winter lots often praised for a thicker, cleaner cup and spring lots for aroma. Shan Lin Xi is less faked than Alishan or Li Shan but the name is still used loosely; a named sub-area, a harvest date and a vacuum-sealed pack are what to look for.

It is a tea for the morning rather than the evening, bright and clearing, and a good first step beyond Alishan for anyone who wants to taste what altitude does.
